task_brief: Day 2 of "Data Representation and Structures" (unit 1, grade 10) is a worked-model trace on arrays and lists. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Implement and measure two data structures for the same task and justify the selection with evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling arrays and lists at the explicit model stage, against the unit's wider topics of numeric text and binary encoding, arrays and lists, dictionaries and records, and stacks and queues. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Work through the complete central input printed in activity_setup for arrays and lists, one step at a time rather than reading it straight through. For each step, write what changed and why that step is legal. Build a trace table with one row per step showing the values or states before and after. Then change exactly one line, value, or condition in the model, predict the new result before running or re-tracing it, and record whether your prediction was right. Explain in your own words the rule that makes arrays and lists behave the way the model shows. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about arrays and lists, and it belongs to "Data Representation and Structures", which also covers separate topics such as numeric text and binary encoding. Close out with this check before you stop: Explain the modelled approach to arrays and lists in your own words and name the step most likely to go wrong. At grade 10 the bar is independent work that justifies its approach against a named alternative you considered and rejected, with the trade-off stated concretely.

central_input.title: Inline arrays and lists code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate arrays and lists; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The query must select active records and total their values; the supplied records must return 6.
Inactive records must not affect the result, and an empty record list must return 0.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to arrays and lists, not merely state the final number.
The boundary test must be completed and its actual result compared explicitly with the expected result.

execution_method.primary: No-install browser method: open any browser developer console, paste the complete starter code, press Enter, and record the output or exact error text.
execution_method.local_optional: If Node.js is already installed, save the unchanged snippet as activity.js and run `node activity.js`; installing Node.js is not required.
execution_method.no_computer_required: The hand-trace route below is a complete execution method and earns identical credit.

debugging_target.observed_failure: The selection is correct, but the aggregation subtracts each selected value, so the supplied records return -6 instead of 6.
debugging_target.target: Repair the aggregation operator, explain the selected rows and accumulator state, and rerun all three tests.
debugging_target.passing_change: The reducer uses total + record.value; the tests return 6, 0, and 0.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to arrays and lists is the central evidence.

equal_credit_alternative.method: Paper or notes-app simulation; this earns exactly the same score as running code.
steps: Make one row for each statement or loop check and copy the starting input exactly.
Record every variable, object field, selected item, and output after that step.
Circle the first row where the actual state stops matching the specification.
Apply the one repair named in your explanation and trace all three tests again.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: The completed trace, the one-line corrected condition, and an expected-versus-actual table for all three tests.

test_or_check_criteria: The trace table has one row per step and shows values or states both before and after that step.
Every step carries a written reason that step is legal, not just a restatement of what happened.
Exactly one deliberate change was made to the model, with a prediction recorded before the re-run and the outcome after.
The rule governing arrays and lists is restated in the student's own words rather than copied from the model.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.
Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, diagrammed, or demonstrated responses; where code is the target, accept pseudocode, block-based, or annotated-trace evidence.
Provide screen-reader-compatible editors, adjustable font and contrast, keyboard-only workflows, and an offline paper-and-trace route for every programming task.
task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting arrays and lists.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for arrays and lists follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for arrays and lists, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to arrays and lists works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of arrays and lists, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking arrays and lists mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply arrays and lists under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on arrays and lists rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
